authors: Wen Yi; Albert P. C. Chan
title: Effects of Heat Stress on Construction Labor Productivity in Hong Kong: A Case Study of Rebar Workers
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 14(9):1055
access: Open access, CC BY (licence text seen on PMC5615592 full text)
country: Hong Kong (two construction training grounds, Aug-Sep 2016; hot-humid subtropical)
trade_activity: Steel bar (rebar) fixing - manual building trade, NOT masonry
modifier_name: Heat stress (WBGT) plus work intensity, work duration, age, alcohol habit -> direct work time (CLP)
equation_text: CLP = 1.602 - 0.028*WBGT + 0.231*%HRmax - 0.035*WD - 0.005*Age - 0.085*ADH  (Eq. 2, as printed with unicode minus signs; WBGT in deg C; WD = work duration in hours; ADH = alcohol drinking habit coded 0/1/2; %HRmax = percentage of maximum heart rate)
output_definition: CLP = construction labor productivity measured as proportion of 15-min direct work time (DWT, AACE direct/indirect/non-productive work sampling, 4114 observations). Absolute output (fraction/percentage of time in direct work), NOT a multiplier on a baseline; the unit of CLP inside Eq. 2 is not stated in the text read, and the abstract's statement 'direct work time decreased by 0.33% when WBGT increased by 1 C' cannot be reconciled with the printed coefficient -0.028 per deg C from the text alone.

fit.other: validation on 38 held-out sets: RMSE 0.857, MAPE 0.092, Theil's U 0.009; max VIF 5.68; 378 sets total, 32 outliers removed

evidence_depth: Full text read (PMC HTML). Small sample: 14 male rebar fixers (mean age 29 +/- 3.32), acclimatised, training-ground not live site.
limitations: Rebar not masonry; Hong Kong not India; small homogeneous sample of young acclimatised workers; unit of CLP in Eq.2 not stated and inconsistent with abstract's 0.33%/deg C; requires %HRmax (physiological measurement) as an input so not directly usable from weather data alone; WBGT needs globe/wet-bulb instrument; validity only 22-35.5 deg C WBGT.

authors: Lendra; Muhammad I. R. Resnawan; Waluyo Nuswantoro; Andi
title: Impact of Overtime Work on Construction Labor Productivity: Evidence from Work Sampling Analysis of Finishing Activities
journal: Journal of Engineering Management and Systems Engineering 5(2):156-177
access: Open access, CC BY 4.0 (licence statement seen on page 1 of the PDF)
country: Indonesia (Palangka Raya, Central Kalimantan; two-storey residential, Jun-Dec 2025)
trade_activity: Plastering and skim coating (finishing trades, NOT masonry); 9 regular hours + 2-3 overtime hours per day
modifier_name: Overtime (2-3 h after a 9 h regular day) effect on labour utilisation rate (LUR) and on volume output per hour

input_variable.name: Working period: regular hours vs overtime (2-3 h following 9 h)

equation_text: No fitted predictive equation. Printed definitions: LUR = t_eff / t x 100% (Eq. 1); Decrease in Relative Activity = (Initial Value - Final Value) / Initial Value x 100% (Eq. 2); LUR difference = Overtime LUR - Normal LUR (Section 4.2.3).

table.input: Skim coating, regular hours (avg of 3 days)

output_definition: LUR = share of 5-minute work-sampling observations that are effective (percentage; absolute, then compared regular vs overtime); volume output = m2 per man-day/hour normalised to the AHSP 7 h standard. Overtime comparison is a before/after ratio (multiplier on output per hour ~1.28 plastering, ~1.49 skim coating as reported by the authors as +28% and +49%), but with only df = 2 and 3 days per trade it is not a fitted multiplier model.

fit.other: Skim coating paired t-test p = 0.031; plastering Wilcoxon p = 0.109; 1,296 observations (864 regular, 432 overtime), six workers, Cronbach alpha 0.87 (observer consistency); authors call p-values preliminary

evidence_depth: Full text read (local PDF held by user). One site, six workers, three days per trade, two overtime sessions per day.
location_in_paper: Tables 1, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 17; Sections 4.2.3, 4.3.2, 4.4; Section 5.3 (limitations). Secondary citation (Putra et al. [24], not read by me): lightweight brick wall installation overtime productivity +185%, +32%, +22% for foreman, labourer, assistant labourer.
limitations: Finishing (plastering/skim coat), not masonry; Indonesia; extremely small sample (df = 2); payment was a down-payment tied to target output which may inflate overtime output; authors state the two results are preliminary; the direction (LUR falls 1-6.5 pts while volume per hour rises) conflicts with classic overtime-loss literature so it must not be read as a general overtime multiplier.

title: Study of relationship between rework and labor productivity in Building Construction Projects
journal: Revista de la Construccion (Journal of Construction) 19(1):30-41
access: Free PDF held locally by user; no licence statement found in the PDF text (open-access licence NOT confirmed; NC)
trade_activity: Brick works (masonry) - Model 2; also plastering (Model 1) and ceramic works (Model 3)
modifier_name: Rework cost (% of item contract price) -> labour productivity of brick works (2-labour crew, m2/day)

input_variable.name: Rework cost in brick works (% of item contract price)

equation_text: Y = 34.36 - 1.71X   (Equation 5; Y = labor productivity in brick works, m2/day; X = rework cost in brick works, %). Chart trendline printed as y = -1.7107x + 34.36, R2 = 0.7823. For comparison: plastering Y = 40.9 - 2.02X (Eq. 4, R2 0.82); ceramic Y = 44.60 - 2.58X (Eq. 6, R2 0.79).
output_definition: Absolute productivity in m2 per day for a 2-labour crew (not a multiplier). A relative modifier can be derived (P(X)/P(0) = 1 - 0.0498 X, my arithmetic from the printed coefficients: 1.71/34.36), but the paper does not print that form. Paper's text says the Eq. 3 template has Y = rework cost and X = productivity, but Eqs. 4-6 define Y as productivity and X as rework cost (internal inconsistency; Eqs. 4-6 used here).

fit.other: F(1,39) = 62.71, p = 0.00; n = 40 observations; t(intercept) 7.11, t(slope) 6.44

evidence_depth: Full text read (user's local PDF). 40 building projects from contracting firms; regression on project-level averages; each of the three models reports n = 40 (unclear whether same projects).
location_in_paper: Section 'Predictive models', Model 2 (brick works), Equation (5), Table 5, Figure 2; means in text; Section 'Ranking of factors' Table 2 (ranking only)
limitations: Palestine not India; rework cost and productivity are project-level company records (data definitions, crew size definition, wall type, thickness not reported in the text read); plotted rework range appears 0-10% (axis) - observed min/max not stated; linear fit through means: at the printed mean rework 4.51% the line gives 26.65 m2/day (my calc) vs printed mean 26.2 (minor mismatch); text once calls the activity 'block works' though titled brick works; cross-sectional association, not causal; productivity of 34 m2/day intercept is defined only by the crew of 2.

authors: Rateb J. Sweis; Ghaleb J. Sweis; Ayman A. Abu Hammad; Malek Abu Rumman
title: Modeling the Variability of Labor Productivity in Masonry Construction
access: Free PDF on iiste.org (Jordan Journal of Civil Engineering); licence statement NOT seen, so open-access status not confirmed
trade_activity: Concrete masonry wall construction (crew-shift level), all projects work content rating 1 (least complex)
modifier_name: Baseline productivity and normal-variation band (control limits) for daily masonry crew productivity; loss of productivity relative to baseline

input_variable.name: Daily crew productivity (work hours per m2 of standardised masonry)

equation_text: Daily productivity_t = Work hours_t / Equivalent Quantities_t (as printed, definition of daily productivity, Wh per unit of work). Control limits per project: UCL = X_bar + 3.14 x M; LCL = X_bar - 3.14 x M, where X_bar = mean of daily productivity, M = median of the ranges (differences between consecutive daily values); baseline productivity = average of daily values below the LCL (process printed on p.206). A regression on (actual - baseline) with binary factor variables is only PROPOSED (Fig. 10), not estimated.

table.value: 0.946 / 1.104 / 1.314 / 0.876 (range of normal variation above baseline avg 0.454)

output_definition: Work-hours per m2 of standardised masonry (lower = better). Baseline = best achievable with few disruptions. Not a multiplier; a relative productivity-loss index can be formed as daily/baseline (my arithmetic from printed averages: 1.104/0.946 = 1.17, i.e. mean daily labour input ~17% above the printed average baseline; UCL/baseline = 1.314/0.946 = 1.39), but the paper does not print that ratio and its text equates baseline with the LCL average (0.876), which conflicts with the Table 2 baseline average (0.946).

fit.other: No regression fitted; 14 projects, Shewhart-type control limits (factor 3.14 from Nelson 1984)

evidence_depth: Full text read (PDF from iiste.org). Descriptive statistics of 14 Jordanian projects; factor regression only proposed as future work.
location_in_paper: Table 2 (Jordan's database parameters), 'Project Evaluation' p.206 (control-limit procedure), Fig. 9-10 (conceptual loss chart / factor quantification); Table 1 (work content scale 1-5)
limitations: Jordan not India; all 14 projects at the lowest work-content rating (1), so no complexity scaling; per-factor quantification (weather, material, congestion, rework, overtime) explicitly NOT done; unit description in text ('20 mm x 20 mm x 40 mm concrete masonry units') looks like a typo for the standard block size; inconsistent definition of baseline (0.946 in Table 2 vs LCL 0.876 in text); no licence text seen.

authors: Edwin Adakole Agbo; Yohanna D. Izam; Calistus Ayegba
title: Quantifying the Impact of Work Environment Factors on the Variability of Labour Productivity in Wall Plastering
journal: Journal of Construction in Developing Countries (Early View provisional PDF, accepted 02-Aug-2021)
access: Open access, CC BY 4.0 (licence statement printed on PDF page 1 of provisional version)
country: Nigeria (Abuja), 25 public building projects, 30-day observation Jan-Feb 2020

modifier_name: Work-environment factors cited on the workday (waiting for materials, congestion, rework, weather, gang size, supervision, etc.) -> loss of daily productivity

input_variable.name: Binary occurrence of each cited work-environment factor on the day

equation_text: Pav - PbL = Var - PbL + PL1*X1 + PL2*X2 + PL3*X3 ... + PL15*X15  (as printed on p.23; Pav = average daily productivity, PbL = baseline productivity, Var = average variation in daily productivity, PLi = loss of productivity due to factor Xi, Xi = work-environment factor cited during the workday). Productivity = input hours / output (Eq. 7, whr/m2); CPV = PV x 100 / baseline productivity (Eq. 8).

coefficients.note: Unstandardised B (Std. Error), standardised Beta, t, Sig from Table 5; units of B are NOT stated in the text read

output_definition: Dependent variable = (average daily productivity - baseline productivity) in whr/m2 (work-hours per m2, lower is better); coefficients are additive losses per cited factor in the same unit, NOT multipliers. Unit is inferred from the model definition, not explicitly stated for Table 5.

fit.other: F(15,137) = 6.201, Sig F change 0.0005, Durbin-Watson 1.346; 152 completed questionnaires; direct observation of 25 sites, average 28 observations per site

evidence_depth: Full text read (provisional PDF via Semantic Scholar mirror). Serious internal inconsistencies noted below.
location_in_paper: Section 5.4 (model form), Table 4 (model summary), Table 5 (coefficients); Table 2 (baseline and CPV per project); Table 3 (RII ranking)
limitations: Plastering not brickwork; Nigeria; unstandardised B values (up to 3.6) are implausibly large next to baseline 0.993 whr/m2 if the unit is whr/m2 (units not stated) - do not use B as a productivity loss without checking the final published version; the text reports standardised Beta values as '% of variability' (e.g. 62.4%) and quotes p-values that differ from Table 5 (e.g. waiting for tools p = 0.150 in text vs 0.015 in table; congestion t = 2.18 with p = 0.011); Table 2 overall baseline printed as 0.963 whereas abstract says 0.993; provisional (not copy-edited) version.

authors: Rod C. Carter (Long International, Inc.), summarising MCAA Bulletin No. OT1 Revised (2011)

journal: Long International, Inc. website article (undated in the text read; not peer-reviewed)

trade_activity: General construction trades (validation across reinforcement, carpentry, BRICKLAYING, finishing works); worked example is ceiling formwork
modifier_name: Composite fuzzy factor model: 17 factors (weather, shift duration, absence, adaptation, day of week, worker condition, etc.) -> relative productivity Wp (1 = standard)

input_variable.name: 17 factors c1-c17 each mapped to a membership value mu in [0,1]

equation_text: Wp = [ ( SUM_{i=1..17} mu_A(c_i) * w(c_i) ) / ( SUM_{i=1..17} w(c_i) ) + 0.5 ]^y   (Eq. 12); sigma_w = (sigma_t)^y (Eq. 13); y = ln(sigma_w) / ln(sigma_t) (Eq. 14). Wp is the relative productivity where 100% = the standard; the +0.5 shifts an average quotient of 0.5 to Wp = 1. y widens the range: printed Table 4 gives the theoretical interval [z1, z2] of Wp for y = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

coefficients.weights_w_from_Table3: 0.25 (low): c3 shift duration, c10 recovery of strength, c14 time with family, c15 worker absence; 0.5 (average): c2 noise, c6 stress, c9 age, c11 precipitation, c12 air temperature, c13 wind, c16 day of week, c17 adaptation; 0.75 (high): c1 ergonomics, c5 workstation organisation, c7 fatigue, c8 health; 1.0 (very high): c4 salary
coefficients.worked_example: all 17 factors, ceiling formwork, 14 Oct 2015: Wp = 1.04; standard 0.769 m2/w-h -> 0.800 m2/w-h; value of exponent y not stated in the text read

table.input: Age x (years): mu = 0 for x<=16 or x>=55; (x-16)/10 for 16<x<26; 1 for 16<=x<=45 [as printed; the printed cases conflict for 26-45 vs 16<=x<=45]; (55-x)/10 for 45<x<55
Noise x (dB): 1 for x<=52; (85-x)/33 for 52<x<85; 0 for x>=85
Shift duration x (h): 0 for x<=6 or x>=12; (x-6)/1.5 for 6<x<7.5; 1 for 7.5<=x<=9; (12-x)/3 for 9<x<12
Recovery ratio T_fo/T (%): 0 for <=6 or >=30; (T-6)/8 for 6<T<14; 1 for 14<=T<=20; (30-T)/10 for 20<T<30
Precipitation x (mm): 1 for x=0; (10-x)/10 for 0<x<10; 0 for x>=10
table.value: Eq. 5 (time basis of the mm value not stated)

table.input: Wind x (m/s): 1 for x=0; (10-x)/10 for 0<x<10; 0 for x>=10
Air temperature x (deg C): 0 for x<=4; (x-4)/12 for 4<x<16; 1 for x=16; (28-x)/12 for 16<x<28; 0 for x>=28
Worker absence x (workdays r-d): 0 for x=0; x/5 for 1<x<5; 1 for x>=5
Adaptation to new working conditions x (day): 0 for x=1; (x-1)/15 for 2<=x<=15; 1 for x>=16
Time with family x (r-d/week): 1 for x<=5; 0 for x>=6
Day of week: Mon 0.38; Tue 0.87; Wed 1; Thu 0.88; Fri 0.84; Sat 0
Linguistic factors (ergonomics, salary, workstation organisation, stress, fatigue, health) trapezoids (a;b;c;d)

output_definition: Wp = relative labour productivity (percent of the standard, 1.0 = 100%); a MULTIPLIER on a standard/baseline productivity rate (worked example multiplies the directory standard 0.769 m2/w-h by 1.04 to get 0.800).

fit.other: Validation: 236 measurements on various sites over about a dozen work types incl. bricklaying; Shapiro-Wilk then Spearman/Pearson correlations; text says strong correlation for all but one work type; NO correlation coefficients printed in the text read

evidence_depth: Full text read via browser pane (MathJax source of Eq. 1-15 and Tables 1-5 extracted from the page).

title: Formula for Determining the Construction Workers Productivity Including Environmental Factors
access: Open access, CC BY 4.0 (licence text seen on the MDPI article page)
country: Poland (Cracow); membership functions from literature and expert judgement, weights from a survey of 142 respondents
trade_activity: General construction work (model validated incl. bricklaying); outdoor work
equation_text: mu_A(x) = 0 for x<=4 C; (x-4 C)/(12 C) for 4<x<16 C; 1 for x=16 C; (28 C - x)/(12 C) for 16<x<28 C; 0 for x>=28 C  (Eq. 7 as printed). Enters the composite model Wp = [ (SUM mu_A(c_i) w(c_i)) / (SUM w(c_i)) + 0.5 ]^y (Eq. 12) with weight w and 16 other factors; the factor alone is not a standalone multiplier.
output_definition: Membership value 0-1 of the 'high productivity' set for air temperature; fed into Wp (relative productivity, 1 = standard).

fit.other: No fit statistics for this factor; whole-model validation on 236 measurements, correlations not printed in the text read

evidence_depth: Full text read (equation source extracted from MathJax).
limitations: Literature/expert-defined triangular function (not fitted to measurements); Polish context; weight is a survey rank; composite model averages memberships so one factor changes Wp only slightly (my arithmetic, y=1 and all other factors at mu=0.5: Wp = 1 + w(mu-0.5)/SUM(w), SUM(w)=9 for all 17 factors). Optimum 16 C and 28 C cut-off are for Polish/temperate conditions and would give mu = 0 for most Indian summer days; not calibrated for tropical climates.

authors: Martina Sopic; Andro Vrankovic; Ivan Marovic
title: Understanding and Quantifying the Impact of Adverse Weather on Construction Productivity
access: Open access, CC BY 4.0 (licence text seen on the MDPI article page)
country: Croatia (Rijeka, Krk, Pazin; 1999-2022 weather records); general construction, not masonry-specific
trade_activity: General outdoor construction activities (concrete, steelwork, earthworks, exterior painting, asphalt, crane operations, scaffolding) referenced when discussing weather cancellation thresholds; no masonry-specific figure printed
modifier_name: Adverse-weather DAY-COUNT model (precipitation >=10 mm, stormy wind, cold/hot days) -> expected number of days per month with at least one adverse-weather event; magnitude of productivity loss is explicitly NOT given by the model

input_variable.name: Monthly counts of days with precipitation >=10 mm, stormy wind (gust >= 17.2 m/s), cold days (Tmin < 0 C) or hot days (Tmax >= 30 C)

equation_text: Inclusion-exclusion for 3 events (Eq. 4, as extracted): a+b+c - (a/d)b + (a/d)c + (b/d)c + (a/d)(b/d)c, where a,b,c = number of days in the month with each adverse event, d = number of days in the month (this is the paper's stated way of estimating pairwise/triple joint-occurrence days from marginal counts, treated as independent). Extended forms for 4 events (Eq. 5) and 5 events (Eq. 6) are given in the JSON 'coefficients' field. Confidence interval for a normally distributed monthly count: mean +/- t(alpha/2, n-1) x s/sqrt(n) (Eq. 11) or mean +/- Z(alpha/2) x sigma/sqrt(n) (Eq. 12).

table.input: Pazin, January (mean 21.63, not normal - no CI)

output_definition: Expected COUNT of days per month with reduced productivity due to at least one adverse-weather event (a day-frequency model). The paper explicitly states it does NOT give the magnitude of productivity loss per day (not 25%, 50%, 75% etc.) - that is left to the schedule planner.

fit.other: Shapiro-Wilk normality test per month per city; 95% confidence intervals via t- or Z-distribution where normal; validated qualitatively by interviews with experienced contractors

evidence_depth: Full text read via browser pane (tables, formulas via MathJax source, conclusion section). No masonry-specific number found.
location_in_paper: Section 2.1 (cited thresholds from other studies, not verified at source); Section on Formulas 3-12 (own model); Tables 1-7; Conclusions (explicit statement that magnitude is not given)
limitations: Croatian climate (temperate, not monsoon); the paper's OWN contribution is a day-count/frequency model only, not a productivity-magnitude modifier; the percentage figures quoted above are this paper's citations of OTHER studies and were not verified at their original source in this run; independence assumption in the inclusion-exclusion formula is a simplification the authors acknowledge is imperfect (weather events 'are not clearly correlated' per their own text, i.e. treated as roughly independent).
